title: Samma-sambuddhassa
hook: you stub your toe and something comes out; for Dhananjani it was the homage
tomorrow: what does it mean to go for refuge if you're not in danger?

segments.voice: Yesterday, arahato: to the worthy one, worthy by deeds, not by birth, and palms joined for a life, not a crown. Today the homage gets its last word, and somebody trips.

Two in the morning, you stub your toe on the bed frame, and something flies out of your mouth before you've chosen a single word. Whatever comes out is whatever you've said most. In the Samyutta Nikaya there's a woman named Dhananjani, married to a brahmin who has no time for the Buddha. One day, carrying food to him, she stumbles. And what flies out of her mouth, three times over, is the whole homage: namo tassa bhagavato arahato samma-sambuddhassa.
screen: `A STUBBED TOE AT 2 A.M.` → `DHANANJANI STUMBLES.` → `OUT COMES THE HOMAGE, THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: The last word is the longest, so take it apart. Samma: rightly, fully. Sam: by oneself. Buddha: awakened, from a root that means to wake up. Put back together: to the one fully awake by himself, with no teacher showing him the way. And now the homage is complete. Homage to him, the Blessed One, the worthy one, the one fully awake. Back in the story, her husband is furious. He storms off to the Buddha, ready for an argument, and asks him a question instead: what do you have to kill to sleep in peace? The Buddha's answer is anger. The husband ends up asking to become a monk. The story doesn't say how often Dhananjani had said the homage before that day. It doesn't need to. A line said on ordinary days was there when she stumbled. That's the use of something like the homage in a plain week: not a spell for emergencies, but a groove worn by repetition, so that when the floor tips, the words that come are the ones you chose long ago. Fully awake is what the line honors; saying it often is how it gets into the reflexes.
screen: `SAMMA, SAM, BUDDHA.` · `FULLY AWAKE, BY HIMSELF.` · `WHAT DO YOU KILL TO SLEEP? ANGER.` · `A LINE WORN IN BY REPETITION.` · then, large: `FULLY AWAKE.`

segments.voice: Chant the whole homage out loud, three times through, the way Dhananjani said it: namo tassa bhagavato arahato samma-sambuddhassa. Keep it slow enough that each word lands, with the breath in the bh and the short and long vowels in their places. After the third time, stay quiet and let the room hold the sound.
Samma-sambuddhassa. To the one fully awake by himself: the last word of the homage. Word seven of a little Pali.
Something to keep: fully awake, and a line worn in by saying it on ordinary days. A whole homage, yours now.

howItsDone: In Theravada temples and homes the homage is usually chanted three times through before the refuges and precepts, by monks and lay people together.

fork.setup: you want a steadying line ready for a hard day next month. what does Dhananjani's story suggest?

fork.reveal: the homage was there when she stumbled because it was already worn in. the story never says how often she'd said it; it shows a line that came on its own.

chat.meaning: Dhananjani's homage came when she stumbled because it was a line she'd said on ordinary days. Repetition wears it into the reflexes.

Dhananjani.meaning: a laywoman in the Samyutta who said the homage when she stumbled

Samyutta Nikaya.meaning: the connected discourses, a collection in the Pali canon

samma-sambuddhassa.meaning: to the one fully awake by himself

brahmin.meaning: a member of the priestly class in the Buddha's India

sources.ref: SN 7.1, Dhanañjānī Sutta (she stumbles and utters the homage three times; her husband asks what one must kill to sleep in peace; the answer is anger; he goes forth)
sammā (rightly, fully), sam- (by oneself), buddha (awakened, from budh, to wake)
sources.work: T. W. Rhys Davids and William Stede, The Pali Text Society's Pali-English Dictionary

notes: SN 7.1 paraphrased: Dhanañjānī, wife of a brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, stumbles (the text has her bringing food to the brahmin) and utters the homage three times; he goes angrily to the Buddha, asks what one must slay to sleep happily, hears 'anger', and goes forth.
